analysis.one_liner: Replaces a strict duty for retirement advisors to act in clients' best interest with disclosure notices, and blocks the Labor Department's rule unless Congress approves it.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have killed the Labor Department's conflict-of-interest rule for retirement advisors by replacing its best-interest duty with disclosure notices, cleared a House committee 22-14 with 38 cosponsors but never received a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Labor Department had written a rule requiring people who advise retirement savers — including on rolling over a 401(k) into an IRA — to act in the client's best interest, rather than merely recommending suitable products while earning commissions. This bill would have rewritten the law to allow advisors to keep earning commissions and variable pay on retirement advice as long as they hand out standardized disclosure notices, and it would have barred the Labor Department from putting its fiduciary rule in effect unless both chambers of Congress passed a law specifically approving it. The bill cleared committee but never came up for a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Commission-based brokers, annuity sellers, and firms selling their own investment products to retirement savers. The bill would have let them continue collecting commissions and variable compensation on retirement advice — including advice to roll a 401(k) into an IRA — under a disclosure regime, and would have stopped the Labor Department rule that imposed a best-interest duty and new legal liability for conflicted advice.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new statutory exemption letting advisors receive commissions and variable compensation on retirement advice if they give standardized notice that fees may vary and that cheaper options exist elsewhere, plus a written description of the compensation involved [S3] [S4].
Allows advice to be based on a limited menu of investment options, including the advisor's own firm's products, so long as a fixed-notice disclosure is given before the transaction [S3] [S4].

Prohibits the Department of Labor from amending the rules defining who counts as a fiduciary, and would block any not-yet-effective rule — i.e., the department's pending conflict-of-interest rule — from taking effect unless Congress passed a bill specifically approving it within 60 days [S2] [S3] [S4].
Retains some investor protection: advisors who breach a best-interest standard or give advice forbidden by ERISA's prohibited-transaction rules remain legally liable under ERISA [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Retirement savers, especially workers rolling a 401(k) into an IRA. Under the bill's regime, an advisor could legally steer a rollover toward higher-fee, commission-paying products as long as the required notices were given — the cost shows up as lower returns over decades, not as a line item. Obama administration economists had estimated conflicted retirement advice costs savers tens of billions of dollars a year.

drawbacks.text: Disclosure is not the same as a legal duty: the bill's exemption keeps conflicted commissions permissible, so an advisor could still recommend a product that pays them more, and the saver's only recourse for ordinary disclosures is the disclosure itself [S4].

It handcuffs the regulator: the bill bars the Department of Labor from amending fiduciary rules and gives any pending rule 60 days to win an affirmative act of Congress, a much higher bar than the usual process where an agency weighs public comments [S2] [S3] [S4].

The strongest good-faith objection from supporters: the Labor Department's stricter rule would raise compliance costs and could push firms to stop serving small savers, which the bill's own title ('Affordable Retirement Advice') and stated purpose reflect [S4].
A practical risk for any firm was that unclear rules could invite lawsuits, which is why the reported bill added 'good faith' protection for disclosure errors cured within 30 days [S3] [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was not purely deregulatory — it wrote a best-interest standard and ERISA liability into law and gave advisors legal certainty — but its central effect was to trade a strong, enforceable duty for printed notices, while permanently blocking the Labor Department's stronger rule. For retirement savers, the expected cost of continued conflicted advice, estimated by the administration's economists at tens of billions of dollars annually, outweighs the compliance-cost savings the bill promised to preserve. The bill was well designed for the firms it protected; the protections it left savers were the weaker of the two regimes on offer.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it 22-14 and it sat on the House calendar, but no one ever brought it up for a vote before that Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 18, 2015 and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S6].
The committee considered and marked it up on February 2, 2016, ordering it reported as amended on a 22-14 vote [S6].
It was reported as amended on April 20, 2016 (H. Rept. 114-511) and placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 391 — the list of bills awaiting floor consideration [S6].
No floor vote ever occurred; the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 with the bill still on the calendar [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retirement savers came out ahead in the narrow sense that the stronger best-interest rule the bill targeted never faced this direct repeal. The brokerage and annuity firms backing the bill gained nothing from its passage because there was none — the Department of Labor's rule proceeded (and was later litigated separately) rather than being blocked by this statute.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Retirement savers; the bill's industry backers gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: The bill cleared committee 22-14 and drew 32 Republican cosponsors to 6 Democratic, so it leaned Republican while keeping a small bipartisan wing; the record does not break down the committee vote by party.

industries.note: The bill would have kept commissions and variable pay legal on retirement advice — including rollover advice — with only standardized disclosures, and would have killed the Labor Department rule imposing a best-interest duty. Their revenue model of paying advisors by product sold would have survived intact.

The fiduciary rule threatened the commissions paid on annuities sold into retirement accounts; the bill's exemption for advice 'that may result in variable income' would have preserved those sales. Annuity commissions are among the highest-fee products retirement savers encounter.

The bill expressly allowed advice based on a limited menu of options that 'may consist, in whole or in part, of proprietary products,' provided a notice says cheaper versions may exist elsewhere. That turns the advisor's shelf into the firm's catalog with a disclosure as the safeguard.
